interactions.summary: Jiang ties the loss of time-awareness to Dante's happiness at escaping hell, then reads the climb and geolocation passage as another father-son scene in which Dante becomes needier and more childish while Virgil keeps him moving.
A student reads the climb, the resting terrace, and Virgil's geographical explanation that Mount Purgatory stands opposite Mount Zion.

claims.claim: Jiang says Dante stops noticing time because he is happy to be out of hell and surrounded by sunlight and hopeful souls.
Virgil geolocates Mount Purgatory as the opposite pole to Mount Zion and Jerusalem, making the mountain cosmologically precise even if the placement feels strange.
claims.temporal_scope: Quoted reading and lecture gloss dated 2026-06-24.

claims.claim: Jiang reasserts that Dante and Virgil now behave like father and son on a hike, with Dante regressing into repeated complaints and Virgil responding like an impatient parent.

signature_moments.moment: The sublime climb briefly turns comic: Dante is no longer just reverent disciple but an exhausted child asking whether they are there yet.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It keeps the guide relation vivid and unstable rather than merely allegorical.

chronology_notes.note: As Dante grows happier and less time-conscious, the poem also makes Purgatory more locatable and more humanly ordinary through the father-son hiking dynamic.
